section_titles: Daisy and Lou Go Shopping
periods.activity_title: Market Maths: Costs, Combinations, and Change

tasks_in_class.description: Find costs for different quantities of fruits/vegetables; find what combinations sum to ₹163 (more than one possibility).
Lou and Daisy buy 3 kg bananas (₹165). Which of the currency options a–e can they use to pay?

homework.description: Complete 9 Cost–Paid–Balance grids by finding the missing value in each row.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the Mawlynnong market scene using the price list on p.97. Children read the prices aloud and handle play-money notes to build familiarity with the denominations. Pose: 'If you buy 2 kg of oranges and 1 kg of tomatoes, what do you pay?' Let pairs compute and share.

Let Us Do, p.97 ("find costs and combinations that sum to ₹163...."). Children work in pairs, listing different fruit-vegetable combinations from the price list that together cost exactly ₹163. Emphasise that more than one answer is valid; pairs compare combinations with a neighbouring pair.

Let Us Do, p.98 ("which currency options can be used to pay ₹165...."). Children examine the five currency-combination options for buying 3 kg of bananas. They check each option by totalling the coins/notes shown and deciding if the total meets or exceeds ₹165. Groups share reasoning.
Quick class discussion: 'Which combinations worked and why? What made some options impossible?' Assign the Cost–Paid–Balance grid task on p.98 as home practice.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is treating the price list as per-item rather than per-kilogram; draw attention to the unit of sale before children begin computing costs. When checking combinations for ₹163, encourage children to record their working systematically so they can confirm no combination is counted twice. The currency-option task sharpens understanding of how notes and coins compose a total.

section_titles: A Strange Puzzle — Change from Oranges
Let Us Play — Magic Triangle
periods.activity_title: Change and Combinations: Puzzles with Numbers 1–6

tasks_in_class.description: Find the balance (paid amount minus ₹42) for Krishna (₹50), Sudama (₹100), Mala (₹200), and Neela (₹500).
Place numbers 1–6 in triangle nodes so that the sum on each side is 9. No numbers repeated.
What other sums can you make with these 6 numbers? Can you make 12 on each side? Can you make 13?

time_bands.activity: A Strange Puzzle!, p.99 ("find the balance for Krishna, Sudama, Mala, and Neela...."). Read the rhyming puzzle aloud. Children write the subtraction for each child: ₹50−₹42, ₹100−₹42, ₹200−₹42, ₹500−₹42. Discuss how regrouping appears in the larger subtractions.

Let Us Play, p.100 ("place numbers 1–6 so each side sums to 9...."). Distribute number cards 1–6 per pair. Children place cards at the six nodes of a drawn triangle and adjust until every side sums to 9. Record successful arrangements.

Let Us Play, p.100 ("what other sums can you make with these 6 numbers...."). Groups try to form triangles where each side sums to 12 or 13. Through trial they discover which totals are achievable; collect findings and discuss what makes a target sum impossible.

Brief share-out: each group announces one target sum they tested. Highlight the pattern: not every total from 9 to 13 is achievable, and the reasoning connects to which numbers sit at vertices versus midpoints.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent slip in the orange-change task is subtracting ₹21 instead of ₹42 (the cost of two oranges); check that children read the rhyme carefully before computing. For the Magic Triangle, children who fix a large number at a vertex quickly reduce their search space — praise this strategy without mandating it. The sum-exploration task (12, 13) is open; accept children's conjectures and counter-examples rather than a single 'answer'.
materials: Triangle outlines drawn on paper or mini-whiteboards

section_titles: Let Us Play — Magic Triangle
Add Up — Addition with Regrouping
periods.activity_title: Triangle Target 10, Then Blocks That Carry

tasks_in_class.description: Use same numbers 1–6 and arrange so that the sum on each side of the triangle is 10.
Estimate the number of teachers going on the trip (24 + 28) before computing.
Estimate the number of children going on the trip (438 + 476) before computing.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Play, p.100 ("arrange 1–6 so each side sums to 10...."). Pairs continue with fresh arrangements, targeting 10 instead of 9. Children who found a sum-9 arrangement try swapping numbers systematically to shift the total. Record and compare different valid arrangements.

Add Up, p.101 ("estimate the number of teachers going on the trip...."). Introduce Dienes-block diagrams using the textbook's 24+28 example. Children first estimate by rounding to the nearest ten, then model with flat tens-rods and ones-cubes: when ones exceed 9, bundle 10 ones into a new tens-rod. Record in the H-T-O column format.

Add Up, p.102 ("estimate the number of children going on the trip...."). Scale up to 438+476. Children sketch block diagrams (hundreds-flats, tens-rods, ones-cubes) and predict where regrouping will occur before computing column by column. Pairs discuss: 'Which column needed carrying? Why?'
Quick check: call out a 3-digit addition (e.g. 257+364). Each child writes their estimate on a slate or scrap paper; compare estimates to reveal the range of strategies used.

periods.teacher_notes: The sum-10 Magic Triangle task often reuses the same arrangement as sum-9 with numbers shifted; prompt children to check that all six numbers are present exactly once. When introducing 438+476, children frequently forget to add the carry digit into the tens column — encourage the habit of writing the carried digit above the column before adding. Estimation before computing is the key habit this unit establishes: resist accepting computed answers offered without a prior estimate.

section_titles: Add Up — Addition with Regrouping
periods.activity_title: Column Addition: From Estimate to Algorithm

tasks_in_class.description: 38 + 16: estimate the money spent on pusaw, then write the final answer after regrouping in the H-T-O boxes.
185 + 125: estimate the trip money, then write the final answer after regrouping in the H-T-O boxes.

homework.description: Preeti's school has 423 children; cousin's school has 178 more. How many children study in Preeti's cousin's school?

time_bands.activity: Add Up, p.103 ("estimate money spent on pusaw, then regroup in H-T-O boxes...."). Children write an estimate for 38+16, then work through the H-T-O boxes: add ones (8+6=14, write 4, carry 1), add tens (3+1+1=5). Verify the computed answer against the estimate.

Add Up, p.104 ("estimate the trip money, then regroup 185+125...."). Children apply the same column method to a 3-digit pair with regrouping in the ones. They draw token diagrams if needed and write the carried digit explicitly above the tens column.

Let Us Do Q2, p.105 ("add by aligning numbers in columns: 32+47 through 534+483...."). Children complete all six column additions independently, showing carried digits. Circulate to check alignment of digits by place value, especially in parts (b) and (e) where digit counts differ.
Pairs swap books and check each other's work on Q2. Any disagreement is resolved at the board. Assign Q3 (p.105) as home practice.

periods.teacher_notes: The most frequent error in column addition is misaligning digits when one number has fewer digits than the other — make the H-T-O grid a mandatory scaffold until children demonstrate consistent alignment. For Q2(d) (476+324), the ones sum to exactly 10: children should write 0 in the ones place and carry 1, not write 10. The Kalakshitij table (T-12, T-13) is available as additional in-class extension; it can be noted in teacher_notes as extra practice: Let Us Do Q1 and Q1 follow-up, p.105.

section_titles: Subtract It — Subtraction with Regrouping

tasks_in_class.description: Estimate the difference: how many more children bought Pusaw than fruit plates (83 − 46)?
Estimate how many children are waiting to visit the Living Roots Bridge (438 − 215).
Ram Chacha: 527 mangoes this year, 264 last year. Estimate then find how many more mangoes this year; use/draw tokens.

time_bands.activity: Subtract It, p.106 ("estimate 83 − 46: how many more bought pusaw than fruit plates...."). Children round to nearest ten and estimate (80−50=30). Then model with Dienes blocks: cannot take 6 ones from 3 ones, so regroup 1 ten into 10 ones. Complete the H-T-O subtraction and compare to estimate.

Subtract It, p.106 ("estimate 438 − 215: children waiting for the bridge...."). Scale to 3-digit numbers. Children estimate first, then work column by column in H-T-O. The hundreds and tens do not require regrouping here; confirm the procedure is understood before moving to cases that do.

Let Us Solve, p.108 ("527 mangoes this year, 264 last year — how many more...."). Children read the problem, write an estimate, then solve 527−264 using drawn token diagrams or Dienes blocks. The ones column requires no regrouping; the tens column does (2 tens cannot give 6 tens, so regroup 1 hundred). Children write and check.
Discussion: 'When do we need to regroup and when do we not?' Children articulate the rule in their own words — subtract ones first; if the top digit is smaller, ungroup one ten into ten ones.

periods.teacher_notes: Children frequently write 'borrowing' from earlier instruction; gently replace this with 'regrouping' and connect it to the place-value exchange (1 ten = 10 ones). A common error in 438−215 is subtracting the larger from the smaller digit in any column without regrouping — the estimation habit helps children spot when an answer is unreasonably small. The column-practice and word-problem tasks (T-19, T-20) can be noted as additional practice: Let Us Solve Q4 and Q5, p.108–109.

section_titles: Subtract It — Subtraction with Regrouping
periods.activity_title: Regrouping Across Columns: Practice and Consolidation

tasks_in_class.description: Ranganna made 639 dolls, sold 531. Estimate then find how many dolls are left; use/draw tokens.
Subtract by aligning in columns: (a) 83−29 (b) 345−123 (c) 763−437 (d) 803−350 (e) 900−328.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Solve Q4, p.108 ("Ranganna made 639 dolls, sold 531 — how many left...."). Children estimate (640−530≈110), then compute 639−531 in the H-T-O column. The ones column (9−1) and tens column (3−3) need no regrouping; confirm the answer matches the estimate, then discuss why estimation is faster for a quick check.

Let Us Solve Q5, p.109 ("subtract by aligning in columns: 83−29 through 900−328...."). Children complete all five subtractions, writing each in H-T-O format. Parts (d) and (e) involve zeros in the minuend, requiring regrouping across two columns — allow children to draw tokens for these if needed.

Display three children's solutions for 900−328 on the board. Discuss the step of regrouping a hundred into ten tens when there are 0 tens: 900 → 8 hundreds, 10 tens → 8 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones. Correct any pattern of simply writing 9−3=6 without the regrouping step.

periods.teacher_notes: The zero-in-minuend problems (803−350 and 900−328) are the hardest in the drill; children frequently write '0−0=0' and bypass the need to regroup into the ones. Encourage them to check: 'Can I take 8 ones from 0 ones without regrouping?' before writing any digit. Token or block diagrams remain a valid scaffold for as long as a child needs them — the goal is correct reasoning, not early withdrawal of the model.

section_titles: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits

tasks_in_class.description: Rami read Panchatantra Tales (236 pages); Kesu read Akbar Birbal, Karadi Tales, and Blue Umbrella. Who read more? How many more pages?
Sumi has read 23 pages of Adventures of Feluda (128 pages). How many more pages are left?
Jaggu reads all 6 books (total pages). He has finished Swami and Friends, Akbar Birbal, and 50 pages of Feluda. How many pages left?

time_bands.activity: Read the community library table on p.110 together. Children identify the page count for each book and practise adding three 2- and 3-digit numbers mentally. Establish: 'What is the total pages Kesu read?'

Let Us Solve Q1a, p.110 ("Rami read 236 pages; Kesu read three books — who read more...."). Children first compute Kesu's total, then subtract or compare with 236. Encourage labelling each step before computing — 'Step 1: find Kesu's total; Step 2: compare.'

Let Us Solve Q1b, p.110 ("Sumi has read 23 of 128 pages — how many left...."). Straightforward single subtraction; children write the equation (128−23) before computing. Use this as a pacing check — children who finish quickly can estimate the answer first.

Let Us Solve Q1c, p.110 ("Jaggu reads all 6 books; finished 3 and 50 pages of Feluda — how many pages left...."). This is a two-step problem: find total pages read (add finished books' pages + 50), then subtract from grand total. Children draw a simple bar or number-line sketch to organise information before computing.
Pairs compare their step labels for Q1c. Discuss: 'Did you add first or subtract first? Does the order matter here?' Reinforce the habit of writing what each step finds.

periods.teacher_notes: Multi-step problems expose a common habit of adding all visible numbers without asking what question each step answers; press children to write a brief label ('total Kesu read', 'pages left') beside each computation. Q1c requires children to remember the page count for Swami and Friends from the table — give a moment for children to re-read the table rather than relying on memory. Accuracy in column addition and subtraction built across the Add Up and Subtract It sections is directly exercised here.

section_titles: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
periods.activity_title: Train Journey: Tracking Passengers Across Stations

tasks_in_class.description: Train problem: how many passengers on the train when it leaves Dadri (after boarding 158, alighting 23, boarding 67, alighting 75 at stops)?
Find the number of people who got off the train at Aligarh (final destination).
Were there more people on the train in New Delhi or in Aligarh? How much more/less?
How many people travelled altogether by the train?

time_bands.activity: Draw the train route on the board: New Delhi → Ghaziabad → Dadri. Introduce the passenger table from p.111. Children read the boarding and alighting numbers at each stop and discuss: 'How do we track the running total?'

Let Us Solve Q2a, p.111 ("how many passengers when the train leaves Dadri...."). Children build a running-total table: start with passengers at New Delhi, add those boarding, subtract those alighting at each stop in sequence. Each step is recorded before computing the next.

Let Us Solve Q2b–Q2c, p.111 ("how many got off at Aligarh; more in New Delhi or Aligarh...."). Children use their running-total table to answer Q2b (passengers remaining = those who alight at Aligarh) and Q2c (compare starting count with Aligarh count, subtract to find difference).

Let Us Solve Q2d, p.111 ("how many travelled altogether...."). This requires summing all boarding events across all stops. Children decide whether to sum all boardings or use a different route; discuss both approaches and verify the answer both ways.
Class debrief: 'What information did we need to keep track of at each station?' Reinforce the value of an organised table when a problem has several sequential steps.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is forgetting to update the running total before moving to the next station — students must complete each add/subtract step before reading the next boarding/alighting value. Q2d often yields over-counts because students add alighting numbers too; clarify that 'people who travelled' counts those who boarded, not those who left at intermediate stops. The running-total table scaffold is more reliable than mental tracking for multi-step problems of this length.

section_titles: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
periods.activity_title: Quick Strategies, Column Drill, and Your Own Problems

tasks_in_class.description: Find quick ways to solve: 326+25, 410−12, 675+5, 204−10, 811+99, 945−19 using strategies from Grade 3.
Find two numbers whose sum is 856 and two numbers whose difference is 563; then make your own word problems with these numbers.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Solve a and b, p.111
tasks_in_class.description: Column addition and subtraction: (a) 452+89 (b) 641−273.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Solve c, p.111 ("find quick ways to solve 326+25, 410−12, 675+5...."). Children work individually for a brief silent attempt, then share strategies with a partner. Collect different methods on the board: e.g. 811+99 = 811+100−1. Discuss which strategy is fastest for each expression and why.

Let Us Solve e, p.112 ("find two numbers whose sum is 856 and two whose difference is 563; write your own word problem...."). Children list possible pairs, check by addition/subtraction, then compose a short one-sentence word problem using their chosen pair. Pairs read each other's problems and verify the answer.

Let Us Solve a and b, p.111 ("column addition 452+89 and subtraction 641−273...."). Children apply the column algorithm with explicit regrouping marks. These two items anchor the procedural skill before the extended home-practice drill.
Assign Let Us Solve d, p.111 as home practice. Remind children to align digits by place value before computing each sum or difference.

periods.teacher_notes: The mental-strategy task requires children to articulate the shortcut (e.g. 'add 100 then subtract 1'); accept multiple valid strategies and avoid endorsing only one. For the problem-posing task, many children write 'what is the sum?' — encourage richer contexts such as books read or distances walked. Column practice on 641−273 will surface any remaining confusion about regrouping across a zero tens digit.

section_titles: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
periods.activity_title: Number Pair Hunt: Greatest and Smallest Sums and Differences

tasks_in_class.description: How many number pairs (adjacent vertically or horizontally) are there in the 4×4 grid?
Find the number pair in the grid whose sum is the greatest.
Find the number pair in the grid whose difference is the greatest.
Fill the missing digits in 3 addition puzzles and 3 subtraction puzzles to make each sum correct.

time_bands.activity: Number Pair Hunt, p.112 ("how many adjacent pairs are there in the 4×4 grid...."). Children first count all horizontal adjacent pairs row by row, then all vertical adjacent pairs column by column. Class agrees on the total before moving to the hunt questions.

Number Pair Hunt Q1, p.113 ("find the pair whose sum is the greatest...."). Children circle candidate pairs of large numbers and compute their sums, then compare to find the maximum. Introduce Q3 in the same band: Number Pair Hunt Q3, p.113 ("find the pair whose difference is greatest...."). Children look for large-minus-small adjacent pairs.

The Missing Digits, p.113 ("fill the missing digits in 3 addition and 3 subtraction puzzles...."). Children use reverse-reasoning: in an addition puzzle, the missing addend is found by subtracting the known addend from the sum; in a subtraction puzzle, the missing value is found by adding or subtracting as appropriate. Work through the first puzzle together, then children complete the remaining five.
Quick class check: invite a child to explain how they found a missing digit in one of the subtraction puzzles. Emphasise the reverse-operation strategy: 'If A − B = C, then A = B + C.'

periods.teacher_notes: Children often miss diagonal pairs in the pair-count — reinforce that only horizontal and vertical adjacencies count. For the Missing Digits puzzles, a common error is treating the blank as always the units digit; children need to read the position of the box carefully before applying the reverse operation. Number Pair Hunt Q2 (smallest sum) and Q4 (smallest difference) are available as additional practice: Number Pair Hunt Q2 and Q4, p.113.

section_titles: Let Us Do — Mixed Addition and Subtraction Drill
periods.activity_title: Full Algorithm Drill: Addition and Subtraction Fluency

time_bands.activity: Brief warm-up: write three additions on the board (one requiring no regrouping, one with ones carry, one with both carries). Children estimate each result and share. This primes the regrouping habit before the full drill.

Let Us Do Q1, p.114 ("add: 23+489 through 826+268...."). Children work through all nine additions in H-T-O column format, writing carry digits explicitly. Circulate and pause at (i) 826+268 (double regrouping) to ensure the hundreds carry is handled correctly.

Let Us Do Q2, p.114 ("subtract: 300−45 through 546−538...."). Children work through all nine subtractions. Items with zeros in the minuend (300−45, 706−209, 600−384, 403−245) are the most demanding; allow token diagrams for any child who needs them.
Self-check: children swap books and mark each other's Q2 using the answer the class agrees on for one chosen item. Any disagreement is discussed briefly — 'What step produced the difference?'

periods.teacher_notes: The drill encompasses the full range of regrouping cases encountered across the chapter — no-regroup, ones-only, tens-only, double-regroup, and zero-in-minuend. Children who finish quickly can be asked to verify selected answers by adding the subtrahend back to their result (inverse check). Q2(i) 546−538 yields 8, which surprises some children who expect a larger answer; estimation (≈550−540=10) confirms the result is reasonable.
materials: H-T-O grid worksheets or squared paper

section_titles: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
Let Us Do — Mixed Addition and Subtraction Drill
periods.activity_title: Smallest Sums, Smallest Differences, and Error Review

tasks_in_class.description: Find the number pair in the grid whose sum is the smallest.
Find the number pair in the grid whose difference is the smallest.

time_bands.activity: Number Pair Hunt Q2, p.113 ("find the pair whose sum is smallest...."). Children revisit the 4×4 grid and circle candidate pairs of small numbers. They compute sums and identify the minimum. Introduce Q4 in the same band: Number Pair Hunt Q4, p.113 ("find the pair whose difference is smallest...."). Children look for adjacent pairs that are close in value.

Return the marked Q2 drill from the previous unit. Children identify any errors in their addition or subtraction work and rework those items, writing the corrected column algorithm beside the original. Peer pairs then confirm corrections using the inverse-check strategy (add result and subtrahend; verify the minuend).

Class discussion: 'Which type of problem was hardest — zeros in the minuend, double regrouping, or tracking running totals?' Children vote and share strategies. Teacher collects common patterns to inform the synthesis unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Completing the Number Pair Hunt's smallest-sum and smallest-difference questions alongside the error-review gives children both fresh reasoning and a chance to consolidate procedural accuracy in the same sitting. When children rework their drill errors, insist they write the full column layout rather than correcting a single digit in isolation — the error often propagates across columns. The inverse-check (add subtrahend to answer to recover the minuend) is a powerful self-correction habit that applies across all subtraction encountered in the chapter.
materials: Marked Q2 drill papers from the previous unit

A Strange Puzzle — Change from Oranges

periods.activity_title: The Cleanest Village: A Whole-Chapter Journey

time_bands.activity: Open with a rapid 'gallery of ideas': the teacher writes on the board the five big ideas from the chapter — computing costs and change, subtracting from round numbers, the Magic Triangle, column addition with regrouping, column subtraction with regrouping. Children call out one thing they remember about each. This surfaces prior knowledge and reveals any gaps before the synthesis tasks begin.

Pose a fresh market scenario: a family visits a village market and spends ₹247 on vegetables and ₹185 on fruits. They pay with a ₹500 note. Children find the total cost (addition with regrouping) and then the change received (subtraction from a round number with regrouping). They write both computations in H-T-O column form with carry/regroup marks shown.

Magic Triangle revisit with a twist: children use the numbers 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 (instead of 1–6) and try to find an arrangement where each side of the triangle sums to 12. They apply the systematic trial strategy developed during the puzzle work — fixing a large number at a vertex and adjusting the remaining placements.

Missing-digits challenge (teacher-composed, not from the textbook): two addition and two subtraction items with one digit blanked out in each, ranging from 2-digit to 3-digit. Children use the reverse-operation strategy: for addition, subtract a known addend from the sum; for subtraction, add result and subtrahend. Pairs check each other's reasoning.

Close with the dissolution question: 'How does regrouping connect shopping money, train passengers, and the Magic Triangle?' Children offer one sentence each. Collect responses to confirm that the core idea — regrouping as an exchange between place-value positions — links all the chapter's contexts.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit assumes all seven sections of the chapter have been taught; it draws on shopping and change (Daisy and Lou Go Shopping, A Strange Puzzle — Change from Oranges), combinatorial puzzle thinking (Magic Triangle), the column algorithm with regrouping (Add Up and Subtract It), and reverse reasoning (Missing Digits). The market scenario in the middle band is deliberately fresh — it is not copied from the textbook — so children must transfer their skills rather than recall a specific worked example. The closing question about the connecting idea of regrouping is the chapter's dissolution test in conversational form.
materials: Number cards 2–7 per pair (or written on paper)

items.prompt: Apples cost ₹40 per kg and mangoes cost ₹60 per kg. Priya's mother wants to spend exactly ₹200. Which combination could she buy?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply each quantity by its unit price and add to check whether the total equals ₹200.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Child computed 3×40+1×60 = 120+60 = ₹180, not ₹200 — did not check the target sum.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Child computed 1×40+3×60 = 40+180 = ₹220, exceeding the target — did not verify equality.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child computed 4×40+1×60 = 160+60 = ₹220, exceeding the target — confused 'at most' with 'exactly'.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child use play money to count out each option physically; stretch: find a second combination that also totals exactly ₹200.

exercise.description: Find costs for different quantities of fruits/vegetables; find what combinations sum to ₹163 (more than one possibility).

items.prompt: Oranges cost ₹55 per kg. Rohan wants to buy 2 kg and pays with one note. Which of the following notes is enough to pay and gives the least change back?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2 kg of oranges costs ₹110. Two ₹50 notes and one ₹10 coin total exactly ₹110, giving no change; all single notes (₹100, ₹200, ₹500) are either insufficient or give more change.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the total cost (2×55=₹110), then check each option's total against ₹110 to find which meets the amount with least surplus.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Child chose ₹200 without checking for a closer option — did not minimise change.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child chose ₹100 without computing the actual cost — ₹100 is less than ₹110 and cannot pay.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Child chose the largest note without comparing options for least change.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use play-money coins and notes to physically count whether each option covers ₹110; stretch: list all single-note or simple coin combinations that cover ₹110 and rank them by the change returned.

exercise.description: Lou and Daisy buy 3 kg bananas (₹165). Which of the currency options a–e can they use to pay?

items.prompt: A triangle has three corners and three midpoints (one on each side), giving six spots in all. You must place the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 — one in each spot, no number repeated — so that the three numbers along each side add up to 9. Write one arrangement that works and explain why the numbers at the corners matter.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One valid arrangement: corners 2, 4, 6; midpoints (on the side between each pair of corners) 1, 5, 3 respectively (e.g. side with corners 2 and 4 has midpoint 3: 2+3+4=9; side with corners 4 and 6 has midpoint 1: 4+1+… — see book for diagram). Any arrangement where each side sums to 9 is accepted. Larger numbers at the corners tend to force smaller numbers at midpoints, keeping sums controlled.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place one number at each node, compute each side's three-number total, and adjust until all three sides equal 9.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child number cards to physically move until a side sums to 9, then fix those three and adjust the rest; stretch: find a second arrangement with a different set of corner numbers that still gives side-sums of 9.

exercise.description: Place numbers 1–6 in triangle nodes so that the sum on each side is 9. No numbers repeated.

items.prompt: Using the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, each used once in a triangle with three corners and three midpoints, which of these side-sum targets is NOT possible?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 13 is not achievable. The numbers 1–6 have a total of 21. Each number appears on one or two sides; the maximum side-sum achievable with this set is 12.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Try to place 1–6 so each side sums to 13; the total of all three sides would need to exceed what the six numbers allow, showing 13 is impossible.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Child forgot that 9 is achievable — perhaps did not try the arrangement or confused the target.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child forgot that 10 is achievable — may not have worked through the puzzle systematically.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Child forgot that 11 is achievable — may not have explored beyond sums of 9 and 10.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child try building a triangle with side-sum 13 using number cards and observe that it cannot be done; stretch: find the maximum achievable side-sum and explain why 12 is the ceiling.

exercise.description: What other sums can you make with these 6 numbers? Can you make 12 on each side? Can you make 13?

items.prompt: Before adding 365 + 248, Ananya estimates the answer by rounding each number to the nearest hundred. What is her estimate?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 365 rounds to 400 and 248 rounds to 200, giving an estimate of 600.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Round each addend to the nearest hundred and add the rounded values.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Child rounded both numbers down (300+200=500) — did not round 365 to 400.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Child rounded both numbers up (400+300=700) — rounded 248 to 300 instead of 200.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child computed the exact answer rather than estimating — did not apply the rounding step.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write 365 and 248 on a number line and mark the nearest hundreds before adding; stretch: now compute the exact answer and find the difference between the estimate and the exact value.

exercise.description: Estimate the number of teachers going on the trip (24 + 28) before computing.

items.prompt: Before subtracting 97 − 43, Bela estimates by rounding each number to the nearest ten. What is her estimate?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 97 rounds to 100 and 43 rounds to 40, giving an estimate of 100 − 40 = 60. Wait — re-verify: 97 is closest to 100 (rounds up); 43 is closest to 40 (rounds down). 100 − 40 = 60. But option B says 50. Re-check: standard rounding — 97 → 100; 43 → 40; 100−40=60. Option C (60) is correct.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Round each number to the nearest ten and subtract the rounded values.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Child rounded 97 to 90 and 43 to 50, giving 90−50=40 — incorrect rounding of both numbers.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child rounded 97 to 90 and 43 to 40, giving 90−40=50 — rounded 97 down instead of up.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child computed the exact answer (97−43=54) rather than the rounded estimate.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: mark 97 and 43 on a number line and identify the nearest ten for each before subtracting; stretch: now compute the exact answer and explain whether the estimate was an over- or under-estimate.

exercise.description: Estimate the difference: how many more children bought Pusaw than fruit plates (83 − 46)?

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt: Meena wants to compute 498 + 9 quickly without writing a column sum. Describe a mental shortcut she can use and give the answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 498 + 9 = 507. Shortcut: add 10 to 498 to get 508, then subtract 1 to get 507 (since 9 = 10 − 1).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Round 9 up to 10, add, then subtract 1 to compensate for the rounding.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child use a number line, jumping +10 then −1 from 498; stretch: apply the same strategy to 597 + 99 and explain why the shortcut works for any number close to a round ten or hundred.

exercise.description: Find quick ways to solve: 326+25, 410−12, 675+5, 204−10, 811+99, 945−19 using strategies from Grade 3.

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt: Write two different pairs of numbers whose sum is 750. For each pair, check your answer by adding the two numbers together.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any two pairs where each pair's numbers add to 750 are accepted. Examples: (500, 250) — 500+250=750; (375, 375) — 375+375=750; (600, 150) — 600+150=750.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Choose one number freely, then subtract it from 750 to find its partner, and verify by adding.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give one number (e.g. 400) and ask the child to find its partner by computing 750−400; stretch: write a one-sentence word problem whose answer requires finding one of these pairs.

exercise.description: Find two numbers whose sum is 856 and two numbers whose difference is 563; then make your own word problems with these numbers.

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt: In a 3×3 number grid, two adjacent numbers are 387 and 456. What is their sum?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 387 + 456 = 843. Ones: 7+6=13, write 3 carry 1. Tens: 8+5+1=14, write 4 carry 1. Hundreds: 3+4+1=8. Answer: 843.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add column by column from ones to hundreds, carrying where the column sum exceeds 9.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Child obtained 833 — likely added tens as 8+5=13 without including the carry from the ones column.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Child obtained 743 — likely forgot to carry at ones, computing 7+6=3 and 8+5=13, mishandling both carries.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child obtained 853 — added hundreds correctly but made an error in the tens column carry.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the numbers in an H-T-O grid and complete one column at a time, recording any carry digit before moving left; stretch: find a second pair of 3-digit numbers whose sum is also 843.

exercise.description: Find the number pair in the grid whose sum is the greatest.

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt:
The addition below has a missing digit. Find the missing digit and explain how you worked it out.

  4 ☐ 3
+ 2 5 8
------
  7 0 1

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The missing digit is 4. Ones: 3+8=11, write 1 carry 1. Tens: ☐+5+1=10, so ☐=4 (since 4+5+1=10, write 0 carry 1). Hundreds: 4+2+1=7. ✓
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use reverse reasoning column by column from ones to hundreds: find what digit makes each column's total match the given answer digit plus any carry.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: work through the ones column together first, establishing the carry, then let the child fill in the tens; stretch: create their own missing-digit addition puzzle and challenge a partner to solve it.

exercise.description: Fill the missing digits in 3 addition puzzles and 3 subtraction puzzles to make each sum correct.

items.prompt: Add 476 + 324 by aligning the digits in columns. What is the sum?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 476 + 324 = 800. Ones: 6+4=10, write 0 carry 1. Tens: 7+2+1=10, write 0 carry 1. Hundreds: 4+3+1=8. Answer: 800.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add column by column from ones to hundreds, carrying whenever a column total reaches 10 or more.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Child obtained 790 — likely forgot the carry into the hundreds, computing 4+3=7.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child obtained 700 — dropped both carries, adding only 4+3 in hundreds and missing the ones and tens carries.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child obtained 810 — may have mis-carried 1 into hundreds a second time or made an arithmetic slip in the tens column.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the sum in an H-T-O grid and circle each carry digit before adding the next column; stretch: verify the answer by subtracting 324 from 800 and confirming the result is 476.

items.prompt: Subtract 329 from 803 by aligning the digits in columns. Show your working and write the answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 803 − 329 = 474. Ones: cannot take 9 from 3; regroup 1 ten into 10 ones (but tens digit is 0 — regroup 1 hundred into 10 tens first). Hundreds become 7, tens become 10. Now regroup 1 ten into 10 ones: tens become 9, ones become 13. 13−9=4. Tens: 9−2=7. Hundreds: 7−3=4. Answer: 474.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Start at ones; when the top digit is smaller, regroup from the next column left, including regrouping across a zero tens digit.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw token diagrams for hundreds, tens, and ones and physically exchange 1 hundred for 10 tens, then 1 ten for 10 ones; stretch: verify by adding 329 + 474 and confirming the result is 803.

items.section_title: Let Us Do — Mixed Addition and Subtraction Drill
items.prompt: Add 826 + 268 by aligning the digits in columns. What is the sum?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 826 + 268 = 1094. Ones: 6+8=14, write 4 carry 1. Tens: 2+6+1=9, write 9. Hundreds: 8+2=10, write 0 carry 1. Thousands: 1. Answer: 1094.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add column by column from ones to hundreds, carrying when a column total exceeds 9, and recording a new thousands digit when the hundreds column produces a carry.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Child obtained 1084 — an arithmetic slip in the tens (wrote 8 instead of 9) or hundreds column; verify step by step.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child obtained 984 — dropped the hundreds carry, writing 8+2=10 as just 0 without recording the thousands digit.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child obtained 1184 — appears to have double-counted a carry or mis-added the hundreds as 8+2+1+1=12.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use squared paper, one digit per square, and write carry digits in a smaller size above the column; stretch: estimate the answer first (800+300=1100) and explain why the exact answer is close to but not equal to the estimate.

items.prompt: Tara buys goods costing ₹78. She pays with a ₹100 note. The shopkeeper fills in a Cost–Paid–Balance record. What is the balance (change) the shopkeeper must return to Tara?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the cost from the amount paid: 100 − 78 = 22.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use play money — lay out ₹100 and physically remove ₹78 to find what remains; stretch: write a new Cost–Paid–Balance row where the balance is ₹35 and find a possible cost and paid amount.

exercise.description: Complete 9 Cost–Paid–Balance grids by finding the missing value in each row.

items.section_title: A Strange Puzzle — Change from Oranges
items.prompt: Leena buys 2 notebooks at ₹35 each. She pays with a ₹500 note. How much change does she receive?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the total cost (2×35=70), then subtract from the note given (500−70=430).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: first compute the cost of one notebook and double it, then use a number line to count up from 70 to 500; stretch: if Leena paid with a ₹200 note instead, could she pay? What would the change be?

exercise.description: Find the balance (paid amount minus ₹42) for Krishna (₹50), Sudama (₹100), Mala (₹200), and Neela (₹500).

items.prompt: A school has 185 children in the morning session and 125 children in the afternoon session. First estimate the total, then find the exact number of children in the school.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Estimate: 200 + 100 = 300 (rounding to nearest hundred). Exact: 185 + 125 = 310. Ones: 5+5=10, write 0 carry 1. Tens: 8+2+1=11, write 1 carry 1. Hundreds: 1+1+1=3. Answer: 310.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Estimate by rounding to hundreds, then add column by column with regrouping from ones and tens.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw Dienes-block diagrams for 185 and 125, combine ones and tens physically, and bundle when 10 are collected; stretch: if 45 more children join the afternoon session, find the new total without re-drawing the blocks.

exercise.description: 185 + 125: estimate the trip money, then write the final answer after regrouping in the H-T-O boxes.

items.prompt: A farmer harvested 527 mangoes this year and 264 mangoes last year. First estimate how many more mangoes he harvested this year, then find the exact difference.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Estimate: 500 − 300 = 200 (rounding to nearest hundred). Exact: 527 − 264 = 263. Ones: 7−4=3. Tens: 2−6 — cannot subtract; regroup 1 hundred into 10 tens: hundreds becomes 4, tens becomes 12; 12−6=6. Hundreds: 4−2=2. Answer: 263.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Estimate by rounding to hundreds, then subtract column by column from ones, regrouping from hundreds to tens when needed.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw token diagrams and physically exchange 1 hundred-token for 10 ten-tokens before subtracting the tens column; stretch: verify the answer by adding 264 + 263 and confirming the total is 527.

exercise.description: Ram Chacha: 527 mangoes this year, 264 last year. Estimate then find how many more mangoes this year; use/draw tokens.

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt: In the school library, Riya reads a book with 236 pages. Her friend Karan reads three books with 98, 115, and 74 pages. Who reads more pages in total and by how many?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Karan's total: 98+115+74. Step 1: 98+115=213. Step 2: 213+74=287. Riya: 236. Karan reads more. Difference: 287−236=51. Karan reads 51 more pages.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add Karan's three book totals step by step, then subtract Riya's total to find the difference.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: add Karan's books two at a time and record each running total before comparing with Riya; stretch: if Riya reads one more book so she reads the same total as Karan, how many pages must that book have?

exercise.description: Rami read Panchatantra Tales (236 pages); Kesu read Akbar Birbal, Karadi Tales, and Blue Umbrella. Who read more? How many more pages?

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt: A bus starts with 0 passengers. At Stop 1, 158 people board and 23 get off. At Stop 2, 67 board and 75 get off. How many passengers are on the bus after Stop 2?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: After Stop 1: 0+158−23=135. After Stop 2: 135+67−75=127. Answer: 127 passengers.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Keep a running total: add boardings and subtract alightings at each stop in order.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a simple table with columns 'Stop', 'Board', 'Alight', 'Running total' and fill it row by row; stretch: if 40 more people board at a third stop and 28 get off, find the new total.

exercise.description: Train problem: how many passengers on the train when it leaves Dadri (after boarding 158, alighting 23, boarding 67, alighting 75 at stops)?
